justification_text:
At the time of the forecast, gold was trading in the mid-to-upper $1,800s per ounce, and my one-day point estimate of $1,895 reflected a modest continuation of near-term momentum with limited expectation of a sharp reversal within a single session. Gold tends to exhibit mean-reverting behavior over very short horizons when there are no major scheduled catalysts, so the estimate stayed close to the prevailing price. The one-week estimate of $1,905 incorporated a slight upward drift, consistent with the broader macro backdrop of persistent inflation concerns, a moderately weak dollar, and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty that had been supporting safe-haven demand. The one-month estimate of $1,920 extended that drift further, reflecting a longer-run environment where central bank policy uncertainty and real yield fluctuations tend to push gold gradually higher when nominal rates are near their peak and markets begin pricing in eventual easing.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly $110 captures intraday and overnight volatility, which for gold is meaningful but bounded absent a major shock. At one week, the interval widens to $250, accounting for scheduled economic data releases such as CPI prints, Federal Reserve communications, and Treasury auctions, all of which can shift real yield expectations and the dollar meaningfully. At one month, the $550-wide interval acknowledges that over a four-week horizon, the macro narrative can shift substantially — a surprise in inflation data, a pivot in Fed tone, or a change in geopolitical conditions could drive gold well outside the central tendency.

The most significant tail risks on the upside would be an unexpected escalation in geopolitical conflict, a sudden financial stress event prompting a flight to safety, or a materially weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs or inflation report that accelerates rate-cut expectations. On the downside, a surprisingly hawkish Fed — whether through statements or an unexpected rate hike — combined with a strong dollar rally could push gold below $1,650 within a month. A rapid de-escalation of geopolitical tensions or a sharp recovery in risk appetite could also compress safe-haven demand meaningfully. These scenarios represent genuine tail outcomes that the stated intervals were not designed to fully contain, as a 90% confidence interval by construction leaves a 10% probability for outcomes beyond its bounds, and gold is a notoriously sentiment-driven asset capable of sharp directional moves.
